512.prompt: Max was tired of finding empty mugs on his desk. That morning he counted five of them, and he thought
512.completion:
that something must be done. So he devised a plan. Every time Max returned from a break, he looked around to see whether all his coworkers were back at their desks, and if not, he looked for people who had come in five minutes after him. If everyone was back, he got a drink. Max kept a record of all the times he got a drink because he believed that everyone would be back after two minutes and thirty seconds, plus or minus half a second, on average. From time to time, Max got some data by doing an experiment which he called ‘observation’ Here’s how it went: 1. He placed all the mugs in a very obvious place on his desk, in rows of 3, the same way every time 2. He left for a break 3. He came back, and he observed what had happened to the mugs. As is well-known, Max never knew whether someone had drunk his coffee or whether he had just forgotten to take his mug with him. His model was that, after 3 seconds since his return, mugs migrated (i.e. got drunk from) at a Poisson rate, independently of each other, with alpha = 1.0. NB1. He had enough mugs for everyone to get one. NB2. He had also read about hierarchical models, generative models and Metropolis-Hastings algorithms, but he didn’t understand much, and he didn’t have time. Sadly, he wasn’t a mathematician, and didn’t want to be. NB3. He didn’t want to look like he was being systematic, and did only one experiment per day. NB4. He mostly had lunch with his girlfriend, rather than in the office, but sometimes he met his coworkers in the park. NB5. Noone else drank his coffee.

1. Calculate the probability mass function (PMF) of the observed states of the mugs under Max’s model, for each experiment 2. Compute the posterior predictive distribution of future states of the mugs, for each experiment 3. Compute the posterior predictive probability of at least one mug being drunk, and at least two mugs being drunk, for each experiment

Tasks: given our model and the observed data

1. Calculate the number of times Max drank his coffee, and show it as a PMF 2. Using Metropolis-Hastings algorithm

Why do we cause ourselves to be sad?

My nerves were being pulled by springy fishing gear. I had a quarrel with my closest friend and now I have to contact my new friends. I had to comfort my friend. I had to do household chores now that my mother is not here. It seems like life is pushing me down, but there is no escape. I feel bitter about life, like water was dripping into my heart. Looking back at my life right now, I see these tiny moments where I cause myself to be sad. Even though I tried to comfort my friend, I still left so many words unsaid. There were times when I felt ashamed of myself because of some things. There were also times when I should have opened up to my parents more. I always thought I was a smart person. But as I've grown older, I've had unexpected challenges. When I was 17 years old, I thought I had accomplished a lot with little effort as I finished a massive amount of work overnight. but in this condition, I must face these tiny moments again and again. I am so tired but I cannot fall asleep as I have to sort out my feelings. My parents supported me silent, yet they were worried about me. I hate myself for always letting things linger and not being able to face my problems. I am not worth someone's investment, but I still believe there are people like a drop of water in my life. I still heard about a beautiful love story, and I still have many childish interests.
